results.content:
What you'll see:
1. Connect Gmail to Clam, not to the agent. Clam sorts your mail into categories like travel, receipts and banking. It doesn't store your emails.
2. Create a Shell, the travel assistant's slice of your inbox, and write its rule in plain English. Clam compiles it into a Cedar policy.
3. Connect your agent to the Shell through Clam's MCP server.
4. Ask it to build an itinerary and draft a reply to a host. Then ask it for something outside the rule, like a bank statement or sending the reply itself, and watch Clam deny it.
5. Open the audit log: every request, allowed or blocked, with the rule that decided it.

Anything the rule doesn't allow is denied. A booking from an airline you've never flown still counts as travel, because rules work by meaning, not sender lists. [...] ## Transcript

results.title: AI agents that can’t escalate are costing you customers - Sinch
results.content:
The same logic applies when an AI agent gets pulled back after a failure. It looks like governance hasn’t paid off, where it’s actually the program working as it should. Across all organizations running AI agents in customer communications, 74% have done it at least once. Where it gets interesting is that among those describing their AI safeguards as fully mature, the number rises to 81%.

Check your inbox monthly for your Sinch Newsletter!

The cause boils down to monitoring rather than performance: fewer rollbacks may just mean poorer visibility into them. Which means the first signal telling a company its AI agent has failed is somebody complaining to customer service… or out on social media. [...] One of the best-known examples is probably DPD’s AI assistant, which in 2024 failed to track a missing parcel, then failed to connect the customer with a human representative, and ended up writing him a poem about how unhelpful it was. That’s the kind of failure that generates immediate customer complaints and public shaming on social media.

But an unhelpful AI agent is harder to spot when it provides a wrong answer with total confidence. In this scenario, nobody asks to be transferred, because they have no reason to. In February 2024, a British Columbia tribunal ordered Air Canada to pay damages after its website AI assistant told a grieving customer he could claim a bereavement discount within 90 days of booking. [...] The company’s actual policy, published on its website, said otherwise, but the AI agent contradicted it anyway, and the customer was later refused the refund. The tribunal found the company liable for negligent misrepresentation, rejecting its argument that the chatbot was a separate legal entity.

These failures haven’t stopped happening, as NBC Chicago reported this month. Confidently wrong answers are a common reason companies pull back AI agents handling customer communications. In the our survey, 22% of the organizations running live AI agents had rolled one back over hallucination or brand risk.

Has a deployed AI agent ever been rolled back or shut down due to a governance failure?

results.title: ‘Everyone's got a free lawyer': AI is making it easier than ever to submit complaints — but UK public bodies are struggling to deal with ‘AI clog’ | TechRadar
results.content:
AI isn’t immune to mistakes, and that is complicating things further. Believing AI to be an expert in all subjects, many are trusting their chatbots to write a perfect, irrefutable complaint — forgetting that AI can hallucinate or reference sources that may not necessarily be relevant.

This is resulting in an ‘AI clog’ that is stretching budgets to the breaking point and causing a significant headache for courts and lawyers who have to sift through correspondence full of AI slop legalese.

## AI correspondence clogs complaints

“Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, told the Guardian, “It is definitely more taxing.” [...] In the pre-AI era, submitting a complaint took time and required research and a level of expertise. This level of effort acted as a natural filter to spurious complaints. But the release of AI chatbots such as ChatGPT to the general public has made it almost effortless to draft and submit a complaint to almost anyone.

But on the other end, human complaints handlers have to sift through a growing number of AI generated complaints with the same regard they would have for a human complaint, filtering out AI slop to get to the bottom of an issue.

In many cases, the complaints are “very long, repetitive and contain unrelated comments or misdirected demands,” Evans explained. “You get some huge ones. The worst one I’m aware of at the moment is about 200 pages long.” [...] # ‘Everyone's got a free lawyer': AI is making it easier than ever to submit complaints — but UK public bodies are struggling to deal with ‘AI clog’

Court backlogs and complaint resolutions are being slowed by AI

- Councils, authorities and caseworkers are struggling to filter through AI generated complaints
- AI makes complaining easier and that is contributing to backlogs in responses and the court system
- Workers are facing growing workloads without any extra budget

UK public bodies are struggling to deal with a veritable deluge of complaints that have exploded in both number and length with many public servants placing the blame squarely on the popularity of AI chatbots.

results.title: AI-Generated Complaints, Requests Flood Government Offices. It's Not Going Well | PCMag
results.content:
Public bodies in the UK are struggling to handle an influx of AI-written complaints and correspondence, which are often long and full of hallucinations, The Guardian reports.

AI chatbots may be useful tools for quickly whipping up an email based on a few bullet points or a single sentence, but when someone else has to read through it to find the point of the email, it can slow them down, especially if it references non-existent sources. That's the problem facing many public bodies, including lawyers' offices, local councils, schools, and politicians, who say they're struggling to respond to everyone, let alone effectively take action on their behalf.

“Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” Hollie Wickens, a senior case worker in a Labour MP's office, tells The Guardian. [...] This AI slop is causing "AI clog," and it's only growing worse as AI agents begin sending out correspondence of their own. Researchers at Berlin's Centre for Digital Governance, the Cooperative AI Foundation, and GovAI have dubbed this so-called "agentic flooding" a serious concern for public-facing bodies.
